blocks.text: The motional emf induced in a rod moving perpendicular to a magnetic field is ε = −vBL. The motional emf as well as other induced emfs can be described in terms of magnetic flux. Consider the experiment shown in Fig. 10.14 again. Let the conducting rod move from position 1 to position 2 in a small interval of time Δt. The distance travelled by the rod in time Δt is x₂ − x₁ = Δx.

blocks.text: Equation (10.20) shows that if the magnetic flux is changing through the single loop of a conducting coil, then the negative of the rate of change of magnetic flux is equal to the emf induced in the loop.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book cites Equation (10.20) here, but Eq. 10.20 is ε = −vBL sinθ. The equation that gives the emf as the negative rate of change of flux, ε = −Δϕ/Δt, is Eq. 10.23.
If there is a coil of N loops instead of a single loop, then the induced emf will become N times.

Although the above expression is derived on the basis of motional emf, but it is true in general. This conclusion was first arrived at by Faraday, so this is known as Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction which states that:
The average emf induced in a conducting coil of N loops is equal to the negative of the rate at which the magnetic flux through the coil is changing with time.
The minus sign indicates that the direction of the induced emf is such that it opposes the change in flux.

blocks.title: For Your Information
blocks.text: This heater operates on the principle of electromagnetic induction. The water in the metal pot is boiling whereas that in the glass pot is not. Even the glass top of the heater is cool to touch. The coil just beneath the top carries ac that produces changing magnetic flux. Flux linking with pots induce emf in them. Current is generated in the metal pot that heats up the water, but no current flows through the glass pan, why?
